science.title: Octopus and cuttlefish suckers may have evolved by repurposing ancient developmental genes
science.description: Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

science.title: Comparative molluscicidal activity of Fe2O3 and CuO nanoparticles against the harmful herbivorous snail Theba pisana
science.description: This study addresses the increasing agricultural impact of Theba pisana, a destructive terrestrial snail pest that causes significant crop damage worldwide. The study aimed to synthesize and evaluate the molluscicidal activity of iron oxide (Fe2O3) and copper oxide (CuO) nanoparticles against this species. Fe2O3 nanoparticles were biosynthesized using Punica granatum seed extract as potential alternative reducing and stabilizing agent under mild conditions, while CuO nanoparticles were prepared by thermal decomposition of CuCO3 at 500 °C for 2 h. The synthesized nanoparticles were characterized using SEM, XRD, FTIR, and EDX analyses. Their molluscicidal activity was assessed against the target snail species under laboratory conditions using the leaf-dipping technique. The results demonstrated that CuO nanoparticles exhibited higher toxicity than Fe2O3, as indicated by lower LC50 values (455.32 ppm for CuO and 703.61 ppm for Fe2O3). Mortality increased with concentration and exposure time. These findings highlight the greater molluscicidal activity of CuO nanoparticles and suggest their potential integration into integrated pest management (IPM) programs for the control of terrestrial snails.

science.title: H3K18 lactylation promotes VEGFR-3-dependent lymphatic hyperplasia and barrier disruption in metabolic syndrome
science.description: The epigenetic mechanisms by which nutrient overload reprograms lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) remain unclear. Here we show that metabolic stress drives LECs into a glycolytic state, producing lactate that fuels EP300-catalyzed histone H3K18 lactylation at the VEGFR-3 promoter, thereby enhancing chromatin accessibility and VEGFR-3 transcription. This epigenetically induced VEGFR-3 not only promotes LEC proliferation but also engages αVβ1 integrin to activate Src signaling, triggering VE-cadherin internalization and barrier disruption. In mice with metabolic syndrome, this axis drives collecting lymphatic hyperplasia with overt junctional disruption, leading to impaired cardiac lymphatic drainage, myocardial edema, and diastolic dysfunction, a pathological phenotype recapitulated in cardiac lymphatic vessels of metabolic syndrome patients. Genetic ablation of VEGFR-3 in LECs or pharmacological inhibition of lactate production with FX-11 restores lymphatic junctional integrity, improves cardiac drainage, and alleviates myocardial edema. Collectively, these findings establish H3K18 lactylation as a metabolic-epigenetic switch that uncouples lymphatic growth from barrier function under nutrient overload, and identify the LDHA-lactate-H3K18la-VEGFR-3 axis as a targetable node for lymphatic dysfunction in metabolic disease.
